VI Andreev spin qubits

VI.1 Linearized model of Andreev spin qubits

We study the non-interacting model for an Andreev Spin Qubit (ASQ), looking at a general equation for the spin-splitting in terms of Fermi velocities of up and down spins. We consider a single ASQ first in a 1D SNS junction with 3 regions for z<−L/2z<-L/2, |z|<L/2|z|<L/2, and z>L/2z>L/2 described by the three Hamiltonians, respectively

HL\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{L}} =(ℏ​vL​kz−μ)​τz+ΔL​(e−i​φL​τ++ei​φL​τ−),\displaystyle=(\hbar v_{\mathrm{L}}k_{z}-\mu)\tau_{z}+\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}(e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}}\tau_{+}+e^{i\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}}\tau_{-}), (67)
HN\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{N}} =[ℏ​(v+σz​δ​v/2)​kz−μ]​τz\displaystyle=\left[\hbar\left(v+\sigma_{z}\delta v/2\right)k_{z}-\mu\right]\tau_{z} (68)
HR\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{R}} =(ℏ​vR​kz−μ)​τz+ΔR​(e−i​φR​τ++ei​φR​τ−).\displaystyle=(\hbar v_{\mathrm{R}}k_{z}-\mu)\tau_{z}+\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}(e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}}\tau_{+}+e^{i\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}}\tau_{-}). (69)

Here we consider a linearized Hamiltonian close to the chemical potential μ≫Δm=L,R\mu\gg\Delta_{m=\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}} of the different regions with ⟨z|kz=−i∂z⟨z|\bra{z}k_{z}=-i\partial_{z}\bra{z} and τi\tau_{i} acting on the Nambu space. Each Hamiltonian above has its respective copy at opposite momentum with negative velocities. We do not include Zeeman fields, but we include a possible difference in Fermi velocities from the up and down spins δ​v\delta v due to SOI. The velocity vv is the average velocity at the given μ\mu, and we anticipate that it can differ from the velocity without SOI.

The Hamiltonians HLH_{\mathrm{L}} and HRH_{\mathrm{R}} are independent of the spin σ\sigma and can be diagonalized only within a given spin subspace without loss of generality. The eigenvalue problem then reduces to a 2×22\times 2 problem in Nambu space (m=L,Rm=\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}):

[ℏ​vm​kz−μΔm​e−i​φmΔm​ei​φm−ℏ​vm​kz+μ]​[|ψm↑⟩|ψm↓⟩]=ϵ​[|ψm↑⟩|ψm↓⟩],\begin{bmatrix}\hbar v_{m}k_{z}-\mu&\Delta_{m}e^{-i\varphi_{m}}\\ \Delta_{m}e^{i\varphi_{m}}&-\hbar v_{m}k_{z}+\mu\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\ket{\psi_{m}^{\uparrow}}\\ \ket{\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}}\end{bmatrix}=\epsilon\begin{bmatrix}\ket{\psi_{m}^{\uparrow}}\\ \ket{\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}}\end{bmatrix}, (70)

where ↑,↓\uparrow,\downarrow refer to the up and down Nambu component, respectively. This Hamiltonian has the general solution:

ψm↑​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{m}^{\uparrow}(z) =Δme−iφm/2ei​z/ξm(Ce−z/lmϵ−i​Γm+D​ez/lmϵ+i​Γm),\displaystyle=\Delta_{m}e^{-i\varphi_{m}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{m}}\left(\frac{Ce^{-z/l_{m}}}{\epsilon-i\Gamma_{m}}+\frac{De^{z/l_{m}}}{\epsilon+i\Gamma_{m}}\right), (71a)
ψm↓​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}(z) =ei​φm/2ei​z/ξm(Ce−z/lm+Dez/lm),\displaystyle=e^{i\varphi_{m}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{m}}\left(Ce^{-z/l_{m}}+De^{z/l_{m}}\right), (71b)

where Γm=Δm2−ϵ2\Gamma_{m}=\sqrt{\Delta_{m}^{2}-\epsilon^{2}}, ξm=ℏ​vm/μ\xi_{m}=\hbar v_{m}/\mu and lm=ℏ​vm/Γml_{m}=\hbar v_{m}/\Gamma_{m}. The coefficients CC and DD are arbitrary constants. We restrict ourselves to bound states, and thus we require the wavefunctions to vanish at infinity, and in the left (right) region we impose C=0C=0 (D=0D=0). Reintroducing the spin degree of freedom, we have the total solutions for the left and right regions

|ψL⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{L}}} =∫d​z​|z⟩​[|↑⟩​ψL↑​(z)+|↓⟩​ψL↓​(z)]​(α​|+⟩+β​|−⟩),\displaystyle=\int{dz\,\ket{z}\left[\ket{\uparrow}\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\uparrow}(z)+\ket{\downarrow}\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\downarrow}(z)\right]\left(\alpha\ket{+}+\beta\ket{-}\right)}, (72)
|ψR⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{R}}} =∫d​z​|z⟩​[|↑⟩​ψR↑​(z)+|↓⟩​ψR↓​(z)]​(γ​|+⟩+δ​|−⟩),\displaystyle=\int{dz\,\ket{z}\left[\ket{\uparrow}\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\uparrow}(z)+\ket{\downarrow}\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\downarrow}(z)\right]\left(\gamma\ket{+}+\delta\ket{-}\right)}, (73)

where α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma and δ\delta are arbitrary constants and

ψL↑​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\uparrow}(z) =ΔLϵ+i​ΓLe−iφL/2ei​z/ξLez/lL,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}}{\epsilon+i\Gamma_{\mathrm{L}}}e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{\mathrm{L}}}e^{z/l_{\mathrm{L}}}, (75)
ψR↑​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\uparrow}(z) =ΔRϵ−i​ΓRe−iφR/2ei​z/ξRe−z/lR,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}}{\epsilon-i\Gamma_{\mathrm{R}}}e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{\mathrm{R}}}e^{-z/l_{\mathrm{R}}}, (76)
ψL↓​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\downarrow}(z) =ei​φL/2​ei​z/ξL​ez/lL,\displaystyle=e^{i\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{\mathrm{L}}}e^{z/l_{\mathrm{L}}}, (77)
ψR↓​(z)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\downarrow}(z) =ei​φR/2ei​z/ξRe−z/lR.\displaystyle=e^{i\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}/2}e^{iz/\xi_{\mathrm{R}}}e^{-z/l_{\mathrm{R}}}. (78)

Here we absorbed the CC and DD constants into α​…​δ\alpha\dots\delta.

In the semiconductor, the Hamiltonian is diagonal in both Nambu and spin space. The general solution for Nambu component τ=↑,↓\tau=\uparrow,\downarrow and spin component σ=+,−\sigma=+,- is

[ℏ​(v+σ​δ​v/2)​kz−μ]​τ​|ψNτ​σ⟩=ϵ​|ψNτ​σ⟩\displaystyle\left[\hbar\left(v+\sigma\delta v/2\right)k_{z}-\mu\right]\tau\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\tau\sigma}}=\epsilon\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\tau\sigma}} (79)
⇔ψNτ​σ​(z)=⟨z|ψNτ​σ⟩=ei​z/ξNσ​ei​τ​z/lNσ,\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\tau\sigma}(z)=\braket{z|\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\tau\sigma}}=e^{iz/\xi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\sigma}}e^{i\tau z/l_{\mathrm{N}}^{\sigma}}, (80)

where ξNσ=ℏ​vσ/μ\xi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\sigma}=\hbar v_{\sigma}/\mu, lNσ=ℏ​vσ/ϵl_{\mathrm{N}}^{\sigma}=\hbar v_{\sigma}/\epsilon and vσ=v+σ​δ​v/2v_{\sigma}=v+\sigma\delta v/2. A total general state for the semiconducting region is therefore

|ψN⟩=a​|↑⟩​|+⟩​|ψN↑⁣+⟩+b​|↑⟩​|−⟩​|ψN↑⁣−⟩+c​|↓⟩​|+⟩​|ψN↓⁣+⟩+d​|↓⟩​|−⟩​|ψN↓⁣−⟩,\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}}=a\ket{\uparrow}\ket{+}\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\uparrow+}}+b\ket{\uparrow}\ket{-}\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\uparrow-}}+c\ket{\downarrow}\ket{+}\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\downarrow+}}+d\ket{\downarrow}\ket{-}\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\downarrow-}}, (81)

with aa, bb, cc and dd arbitrary constants. If we neglect any flipping of the spin upon reflection at the superconducting-semiconducting interfaces, then we can discard the spin-down components of the total wavefunction, and solve the simultaneous boundary conditions only for the |↑⟩​|+⟩\ket{\uparrow}\ket{+} and |↓⟩​|+⟩\ket{\downarrow}\ket{+} components. This is equivalent to setting β=δ=0\beta=\delta=0 and b=d=0b=d=0 and gives the following four continuity conditions at |z|=L/2|z|=L/2:

γ​ψR↑​(L2)\displaystyle\gamma\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\uparrow}\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) =a​ψN↑⁣+​(L2),\displaystyle=a\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\uparrow+}\left(\frac{L}{2}\right), γ​ψR↓​(L2)\displaystyle\gamma\psi_{\mathrm{R}}^{\downarrow}\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) =c​ψN↓⁣+​(L2),\displaystyle=c\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\downarrow+}\left(\frac{L}{2}\right), (82)
α​ψL↑​(−L2)\displaystyle\alpha\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\uparrow}\left(-\frac{L}{2}\right) =a​ψN↑⁣+​(−L2),\displaystyle=a\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\uparrow+}\left(-\frac{L}{2}\right), α​ψL↓​(−L2)\displaystyle\alpha\psi_{\mathrm{L}}^{\downarrow}\left(-\frac{L}{2}\right) =c​ψN↓⁣+​(−L2).\displaystyle=c\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\downarrow+}\left(-\frac{L}{2}\right). (83)

From Eqs. (82) and (83) we obtain, respectively

ac\displaystyle\frac{a}{c} =ΔRϵ−i​ΓRe−i​φRe−iL/lN+,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}}{\epsilon-i\Gamma_{\mathrm{R}}}e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}}e^{-iL/l_{\mathrm{N}}^{+}}, (84)
ac\displaystyle\frac{a}{c} =ΔLϵ+i​ΓL​e−i​φL​ei​L/lN+,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}}{\epsilon+i\Gamma_{\mathrm{L}}}e^{-i\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}}e^{iL/l_{\mathrm{N}}^{+}}, (85)

which leads to the general solution for ϵ\epsilon, assuming ΔR=ΔL=Δ\Delta_{\mathrm{R}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}=\Delta:

ϵ​sin⁡(ϵ/EL−φ/2)=Δ2−ϵ2​cos⁡(ϵ/EL−φ/2),\epsilon\sin\left(\epsilon/E_{L}-\varphi/2\right)=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-\epsilon^{2}}\cos\left(\epsilon/E_{L}-\varphi/2\right), (86)

where EL=ℏ​v+/LE_{L}=\hbar v_{+}/L and φ=φL−φR\varphi=\varphi_{\mathrm{L}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{R}}. The same equation also holds for the spin-down level with v+v_{+} replaced by v−v_{-}, and agrees with Reference 6 in the short junction limit at perfect transparency. Taking the square followed by an arccos\arccos function on both sides of (86) leads to the alternative formulation [7]:

arccos⁡(ϵΔ)−ϵEL=−φ2+n​π,\arccos\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\Delta}\right)-\frac{\epsilon}{E_{L}}=-\frac{\varphi}{2}+n\pi, (87)

where nn is an integer.

VI.2 Spin splitting

We now analyze the solutions to the transcendental equation (86) and their variations with respect to small changes in Fermi velocities due to SOI. We first re-write (86) in terms of the dimensionless constants x=ϵ/Δ∈[−1,1]x=\epsilon/\Delta\in[-1,1] and α=L​Δ/(ℏ​v)\alpha=L\Delta/(\hbar v) where vv could be any Fermi velocity, and we define the function fα​(x)f_{\alpha}(x):

fα​(x)=x​tan⁡(α​x−φ/2)−1−x2.f_{\alpha}(x)=x\tan(\alpha x-\varphi/2)-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}. (88)

Solving fα​(x0)=0f_{\alpha}(x_{0})=0 for x0x_{0} also solves (86) with ϵ=x0​Δ\epsilon=x_{0}\Delta. A small variation in the Fermi velocity will result in a small variation δ​α\delta\alpha of the parameter α\alpha: α→α+δ​α\alpha\to\alpha+\delta\alpha. Under such a change the function fα​(x)f_{\alpha}(x) becomes

fα+δ​α​(x)\displaystyle f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x) =fα​(x)+dd​α​fα​(x)​δ​α+𝒪⁡(δ​α2)\displaystyle=f_{\alpha}(x)+\frac{d}{d\alpha}f_{\alpha}(x)\delta\alpha+\mathcal{O}(\delta\alpha^{2}) (89)
=x​tan⁡(α​x−φ/2)​[1+δ​α​x​tan⁡(α​x−φ/2)]−1−x2+δ​α​x2+𝒪⁡(δ​α2).\displaystyle=x\tan\left(\alpha x-\varphi/2\right)\left[1+\delta\alpha x\tan\left(\alpha x-\varphi/2\right)\right]-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+\delta\alpha x^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\delta\alpha^{2}). (90)

Evaluating fα+δ​α​(x)f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x) at x=x0x=x_{0} gives fα+δ​α​(x0)=δ​α+𝒪⁡(δ​α2)f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x_{0})=\delta\alpha+\mathcal{O}(\delta\alpha^{2}). The new zero x1x_{1} of the function fα+δ​α​(x)f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x) can be estimated by one iteration of the Newton method:

x1\displaystyle x_{1} ≈x0−fα+δ​α​(x0)dd​x​fα+δ​α​(x)|x=x0\displaystyle\approx x_{0}-\frac{f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x_{0})}{\left.\frac{d}{dx}f_{\alpha+\delta\alpha}(x)\right|_{x=x_{0}}} (91)
=x0​[1−δ​α​1−x02(1+α​1−x02)​(1+2​δ​α​1−x02)].\displaystyle=x_{0}\left[1-\frac{\delta\alpha\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}}{\left(1+\alpha\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}\right)\left(1+2\delta\alpha\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}\right)}\right]. (92)

If the shift in α\alpha for the spin-up branch is α→α−δ​α+\alpha\to\alpha-\delta\alpha_{+} and the shift in the spin-down branch is α→α+δ​α−\alpha\to\alpha+\delta\alpha_{-}, then the difference of the two shifted zeros x1−−x1+x_{1}^{-}-x_{1}^{+} is proportional to the ASQ spin splitting due to SOI:

x1−−x1+=−x0​1−x021+α​1−x02​[δ​α++δ​α−(1−2​δ​α+​1−x02)​(1+2​δ​α−​1−x02)].x_{1}^{-}-x_{1}^{+}=-\frac{x_{0}\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}}{1+\alpha\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}}\left[\frac{\delta\alpha_{+}+\delta\alpha_{-}}{\left(1-2\delta\alpha_{+}\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}\right)\left(1+2\delta\alpha_{-}\sqrt{1-x_{0}^{2}}\right)}\right]. (93)

If v0v_{0} is the velocity without SOI, then we generally expect the following for the velocities v±v_{\pm}:

v+\displaystyle v_{+} =v0+vd+δ​v/2,\displaystyle=v_{0}+v_{d}+\delta v/2, (94)
v−\displaystyle v_{-} =v0+vd−δ​v/2,\displaystyle=v_{0}+v_{d}-\delta v/2, (95)

where vdv_{d} is a SOI-induced velocity drift that is identical for both spins. If fα​(x0)=0f_{\alpha}(x_{0})=0 where α\alpha and x0x_{0} pertain to the drifted velocity v≡v0+vdv\equiv v_{0}+v_{d}, then the changes in velocity ±δv/2\pm\delta v/2 are symmetrical with respect to vv and the variations in α\alpha become

δ​α+\displaystyle\delta\alpha_{+} =L​Δℏ​(1v−1v+δ​v/2)=α⁡(δ​v/2v+δ​v/2),\displaystyle=\frac{L\Delta}{\hbar}\left(\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{v+\delta v/2}\right)=\alpha\left(\frac{\delta v/2}{v+\delta v/2}\right), (96)
δ​α−\displaystyle\delta\alpha_{-} =L​Δℏ​(1v−δ​v/2−1v)=α⁡(δ​v/2v−δ​v/2).\displaystyle=\frac{L\Delta}{\hbar}\left(\frac{1}{v-\delta v/2}-\frac{1}{v}\right)=\alpha\left(\frac{\delta v/2}{v-\delta v/2}\right). (97)

Inserting δ​α±\delta\alpha_{\pm} into the bracket of Eq. (93) and expanding with respect to δ​v\delta v gives the ASQ spin splitting formula for arbitrary junction length LL:

δ​ϵ≡ϵ−−ϵ+=(−ϵ/v1+EL/Γ)​δ​v+𝒪⁡(δ​v3),\delta\epsilon\equiv\epsilon_{-}-\epsilon_{+}=\left(\frac{-\epsilon/v}{1+E_{L}/\Gamma}\right)\delta v+\mathcal{O}\left(\delta v^{3}\right), (98)

where Γ=Δ2−ϵ2\Gamma=\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-\epsilon^{2}} and EL=ℏ​v/LE_{L}=\hbar v/L. Here ϵ\epsilon is the bound state energy of the system computed for the average velocity between those with SOI, i.e. v=(v++v−)/2v=(v_{+}+v_{-})/2. This equation is equivalent to Eq. (4) in the main text.

In the short junction limit α≪1\alpha\ll 1, we can assume that the solution x0x_{0} of fα​(x0)=0f_{\alpha}(x_{0})=0 takes the general form

x0=c0+c1​α+c2​α2+…x_{0}=c_{0}+c_{1}\alpha+c_{2}\alpha^{2}+\dots (99)

Inserting this in fα​(x)f_{\alpha}(x), expanding in terms of α\alpha and setting the condition fα​(x0)=0f_{\alpha}(x_{0})=0 results in the following cic_{i} coefficients:

c0\displaystyle c_{0} =−cos⁡(φ/2),\displaystyle=-\cos(\varphi/2), (100a)
c1\displaystyle c_{1} =sin⁡(φ)/2,\displaystyle=\sin(\varphi)/2, (100b)
c2\displaystyle c_{2} =18​[cos⁡(φ/2)+3​cos⁡(3​φ/2)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}\left[\cos(\varphi/2)+3\cos(3\varphi/2)\right], (100c)
c3\displaystyle c_{3} =−16​[sin⁡(φ)+2​sin⁡(2​φ)],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{6}\left[\sin(\varphi)+2\sin(2\varphi)\right], (100d)
…\displaystyle\dots

Neglecting α3\alpha^{3} terms and higher, the difference of zeros x0±x_{0}^{\pm} becomes

x0−−x0+≈12​(α−−α+)​sin⁡φ+18​(α−2−α+2)​[cos⁡(φ/2)+3​cos⁡(3​φ/2)],x_{0}^{-}-x_{0}^{+}\approx\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_{-}-\alpha_{+}\right)\sin\varphi+\frac{1}{8}\left(\alpha_{-}^{2}-\alpha_{+}^{2}\right)\left[\cos(\varphi/2)+3\cos(3\varphi/2)\right], (101)

which to lowest order in δ​v\delta v leads to the spin splitting provided in the main text [see Eq. (5)]:

δ​ϵ≈L​Δ22​ℏ​{sin⁡(φ)+L​Δ2​ℏ​v​[cos⁡(φ2)+3​cos⁡(3​φ2)]}​δ​vv2+𝒪⁡(δ​v3).\delta\epsilon\approx\frac{L\Delta^{2}}{2\hbar}\left\{\sin(\varphi)+\frac{L\Delta}{2\hbar v}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\varphi}{2}\right)+3\cos\left(\frac{3\varphi}{2}\right)\right]\right\}\frac{\delta v}{v^{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\delta v^{3}). (102)

The approximation sign in (102) comes from neglecting α3\alpha^{3} and higher terms.

VI.3 Expansion of velocities in terms of subband parameters

We consider here a wide junction, such that confinement effects along the xx-direction can be neglected. In Ge, the ASQ still presents a difference in Fermi velocity arising from the cubic SOI. To model this situation, we integrate out the xx-direction by taking the kx=0k_{x}=0 limit of the dispersion relation.

The effective low-energy Hamiltonian of the HH ground state at kx=0k_{x}=0 and arbitrary kyk_{y} can be generally written as a sum of powers of k≡kyk\equiv k_{y}, with the linear-in-kk term omitted due to its small magnitude:

ℋeffσ​(k)=∑i=2ci​ki​σi,\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\sigma}(k)=\sum_{i=2}{c_{i}k^{i}\sigma^{i}}, (103)

where σ=±1\sigma=\pm 1 is the pseudo-spin with σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1. Fixing the energy at a given chemical potential μ\mu and inverting the series (103) for the two pseudo-spins, we get an expansion for kk in terms of powers of μ\mu:

kσ​(μ)=∑j=1ajσ​μj/2,k_{\sigma}(\mu)=\sum_{j=1}{a_{j}^{\sigma}\mu^{j/2}}, (104)

where the ajσa_{j}^{\sigma} are expansion coefficients that depend on the cic_{i}’s. The first four terms are

kσ​(μ)=1c21/2​μ1/2+σ2​c22​c3​μ+18​c27/2​(5​c32−4​c2​c4)​μ3/2−σ2​c25​(2​c33−3​c2​c3​c4+c22​c5)​μ2+𝒪⁡(μ5/2).k_{\sigma}(\mu)=\frac{1}{c_{2}^{1/2}}\mu^{1/2}+\frac{\sigma}{2c_{2}^{2}}c_{3}\mu+\frac{1}{8c_{2}^{7/2}}\left(5c_{3}^{2}-4c_{2}c_{4}\right)\mu^{3/2}-\frac{\sigma}{2c_{2}^{5}}\left(2c_{3}^{3}-3c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}+c_{2}^{2}c_{5}\right)\mu^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{5/2}\right). (105)

On the other hand, the velocity vσv_{\sigma} is given by

vσ≡1ℏ​d​ℋeffσ​(k)d​k=1ℏ​∑i=2i​ci​ki−1​σi.v_{\sigma}\equiv\frac{1}{\hbar}\frac{d\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\sigma}(k)}{dk}=\frac{1}{\hbar}\sum_{i=2}{ic^{i}k^{i-1}\sigma^{i}}. (106)

We recall the following relations pertaining to the spin-dependent velocities:

v+\displaystyle v_{+} =v0+vd+δ​v/2,\displaystyle=v_{0}+v_{d}+\delta v/2, (107a)
v−\displaystyle v_{-} =v0+vd−δ​v/2,\displaystyle=v_{0}+v_{d}-\delta v/2, (107b)

where v0v_{0} is the velocity without SOI (corresponding to all odd-kk powers in ℋeffσ​(k)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\sigma}(k) set to zero), vdv_{d} is a velocity drift that is the same for both spins and δ​v\delta v is the difference of Fermi velocities. Inserting kσ​(μ)k_{\sigma}(\mu) into the velocities gives their expansions in powers of μ\mu:

ℏ​v0\displaystyle\hbar v_{0} =2​c21/2​μ1/2+3​c4c23/2​μ3/2+𝒪⁡(μ5/2),\displaystyle=2c_{2}^{1/2}\mu^{1/2}+\frac{3c_{4}}{c_{2}^{3/2}}\mu^{3/2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{5/2}\right), (108a)
ℏ​δ​v\displaystyle\hbar\delta v =4​c3c2​μ+1c24​(5​c33−12​c2​c3​c4+8​c22​c5)​μ2+𝒪⁡(μ3),\displaystyle=\frac{4c_{3}}{c_{2}}\mu+\frac{1}{c_{2}^{4}}\left(5c_{3}^{3}-12c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}+8c_{2}^{2}c_{5}\right)\mu^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{3}\right), (108b)
ℏ​vd\displaystyle\hbar v_{d} =−7​c324​c25/2​μ3/2+𝒪⁡(μ5/2),\displaystyle=-\frac{7c_{3}^{2}}{4c_{2}^{5/2}}\mu^{3/2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{5/2}\right), (108c)
δ​vv\displaystyle\frac{\delta v}{v} =2​c3c23/2​μ1/2+14​c29/2​(17​c33−36​c2​c3​c4+16​c22​c5)​μ3/2+𝒪⁡(μ5/2),\displaystyle=\frac{2c_{3}}{c_{2}^{3/2}}\mu^{1/2}+\frac{1}{4c_{2}^{9/2}}\left(17c_{3}^{3}-36c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}+16c_{2}^{2}c_{5}\right)\mu^{3/2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{5/2}\right), (108d)
δ​vℏ​v2\displaystyle\frac{\delta v}{\hbar v^{2}} =c3c22+1c25​(4​c33−6​c2​c3​c4+2​c22​c5)​μ\displaystyle=\frac{c_{3}}{c_{2}^{2}}+\frac{1}{c_{2}^{5}}\left(4c_{3}^{3}-6c_{2}c_{3}c_{4}+2c_{2}^{2}c_{5}\right)\mu (108e)
+3c28​(7​c35−20​c2​c33​c4+10​c22​c32​c5+10​c22​c3​c42−4​c23​c3​c6−4​c23​c4​c5+c24​c7)​μ2+𝒪⁡(μ3).\displaystyle+\frac{3}{c_{2}^{8}}\left(7c_{3}^{5}-20c_{2}c_{3}^{3}c_{4}+10c_{2}^{2}c_{3}^{2}c_{5}+10c_{2}^{2}c_{3}c_{4}^{2}-4c_{2}^{3}c_{3}c_{6}-4c_{2}^{3}c_{4}c_{5}+c_{2}^{4}c_{7}\right)\mu^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\mu^{3}\right).

One can replace the cic_{i} coefficients with the corresponding ones from (50): c2=α0​γc_{2}=\alpha_{0}\gamma and c3=α0​β~c_{3}=\alpha_{0}\tilde{\beta}, where β~=−β2+β3\tilde{\beta}=-\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}. We point out that (50) is only cubic in kk and thus cannot capture the contributions from c4c_{4} and above. An exact description of velocities up to cic_{i} requires a iith order SWT on (29).

VII Quantum dot Spin qubits

VII.1 Model

The Hamiltonian of the quantum dot (QD) system is given by (29) or (54) with V∥​(x,y)V_{\parallel}(x,y) given by an effective parabolic potential with effective lengths lxl_{x} and lyl_{y}:

V∥​(x,y)=−α0​(x2lx4+y2ly4).V_{\parallel}(x,y)=-\alpha_{0}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{l_{x}^{4}}+\frac{y^{2}}{l_{y}^{4}}\right). (109)

where the minus sign comes from our electron-energy convention. We first write the Hamiltonian at B=0B=0 and diagonalize it by the usual ladder operator approach. At B=0B=0 the Hamiltonian is

ℋ0qd=ℰ0qw+α0​[ℳγ​k∥2+(i​ℳ1​k−+ℳ2​k−2+h.c.)]−α0​(x2lx4+y2ly4).\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}}=\mathcal{E}_{0}^{\mathrm{qw}}+\alpha_{0}\left[\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}k_{\parallel}^{2}+\left(i\mathcal{M}_{1}k_{-}+\mathcal{M}_{2}k_{-}^{2}+\text{h.c.}\right)\right]-\alpha_{0}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{l_{x}^{4}}+\frac{y^{2}}{l_{y}^{4}}\right). (110)

The ℳ\mathcal{M}-matrices are computed following the method described in Section III. It is a 22nd order SWT Hamiltonian for the first 33 quantum well spin doublets (first 2 H levels and first η\upeta{} level, 𝒜={H​1,H​2,η​1}\mathcal{A}=\{\text{H}{1},\text{H}{2},\upeta{1}\}) computed from a total space of 250250 quantum well subbands. This effective Hamiltonian is the only one that includes an η\upeta{} level in the 𝒜\mathcal{A}-set whose band structure does not bend down at large k∥k_{\parallel} for both unspiked and spiked Ge. For ε\varepsilon-Ge we use the same approach but with 𝒜={H​1,H​2,η​1,η​2}\mathcal{A}=\{\text{H}{1},\text{H}{2},\upeta{1},\upeta{2}\}, also computed from a total space of 250250 quantum well subbands. We write the position and momentum operators with the following ladder operators:

a1\displaystyle a_{1} =ρ−l+i​l​k−2,\displaystyle=\frac{\rho_{-}}{l}+\frac{ilk_{-}}{2}, a2\displaystyle a_{2} =ρ+l+i​l​k+2,\displaystyle=\frac{\rho_{+}}{l}+\frac{ilk_{+}}{2}, (111)
⇔ρ−\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\rho_{-} =l2​(a1+a2†),\displaystyle=\frac{l}{2}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}^{\dagger}\right), k−\displaystyle k_{-} =1i​l​(a1−a2†),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{il}\left(a_{1}-a_{2}^{\dagger}\right), (112)

where ρ±=(x±i​y)/2\rho_{\pm}=(x\pm iy)/2 and

1l4=12​(1lx4+1ly4).\frac{1}{l^{4}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{l_{x}^{4}}+\frac{1}{l_{y}^{4}}\right). (113)

The aia_{i}, ρ±\rho_{\pm} and k±k_{\pm} satisfy the following commutation rules:

[ai,aj†]\displaystyle[a_{i},a_{j}^{\dagger}] =δi,j,\displaystyle=\delta_{i,j}, [ρ±,k±]\displaystyle[\rho_{\pm},k_{\pm}] =0,\displaystyle=0, [ρ±,k∓]\displaystyle[\rho_{\pm},k_{\mp}] =i.\displaystyle=i. (114)

In terms of ρ±\rho_{\pm}, the potential becomes

V∥​(x,y)=−α0l4​[4​ρ−​ρ++2​(ρ−2+ρ+2)​cos⁡ξ],V_{\parallel}(x,y)=-\frac{\alpha_{0}}{l^{4}}\left[4\rho_{-}\rho_{+}+2\left(\rho_{-}^{2}+\rho_{+}^{2}\right)\cos\xi\right], (115)

with ξ=2​arctan⁡(lx2/ly2)∈[0,π]\xi=2\arctan(l_{x}^{2}/l_{y}^{2})\in[0,\pi]. Finally, mutual eigenstates |n1,n2⟩\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} of a1†​a1a_{1}^{\dagger}a_{1} and a2†​a2a_{2}^{\dagger}a_{2} (with integers ni≥0n_{i}\geq 0) are also eigenstates of the angular momentum Lz=x​ky−y​kxL_{z}=xk_{y}-yk_{x}. This is summarized as follow:

a1​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{1}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n1​|n1−1,n2⟩,\displaystyle=\sqrt{n_{1}}\ket{n_{1}-1,n_{2}}, a2​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{2}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n2​|n1,n2−1⟩,\displaystyle=\sqrt{n_{2}}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}-1}, (116)
a1†​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{1}^{\dagger}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n1+1​|n1+1,n2⟩,\displaystyle=\sqrt{n_{1}+1}\ket{n_{1}+1,n_{2}}, a2†​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{2}^{\dagger}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n2+1​|n1,n2+1⟩,\displaystyle=\sqrt{n_{2}+1}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}+1}, (117)
a1†​a1​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{1}^{\dagger}a_{1}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n1​|n1,n2⟩,\displaystyle=n_{1}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}}, a2†​a2​|n1,n2⟩\displaystyle a_{2}^{\dagger}a_{2}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}} =n2​|n1,n2⟩,\displaystyle=n_{2}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}}, (118)
Lz​|n1,n2⟩=(n1−n2)​|n1,n2⟩.L_{z}\ket{n_{1},n_{2}}=(n_{1}-n_{2})\ket{n_{1},n_{2}}. (119)

One can also define the quantum numbers j≡n1+n2j\equiv n_{1}+n_{2} and m≡n1−n2m\equiv n_{1}-n_{2} and write Lz​|j,m⟩=m​|j,m⟩L_{z}\ket{j,m}=m\ket{j,m}, where j=0,1,…j=0,1,\dots and m=−j,−j+2,…,j−2,jm=-j,-j+2,\dots,j-2,j.

To diagonalize ℋ0qd\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}} we project it down onto a basis consisting of all the shells from j=0j=0 up to j=20j=20 (total 231231 spin doublets). The uncertainty on the in-plane momentum ⟨k∥2⟩=1l​1+j\sqrt{\braket{k_{\parallel}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{l}\sqrt{1+j} with j=20j=20 and l=11.2​nml=11.2\,\mathrm{nm} samples regions in kk-space as far as k∥∼0.41​nm−1k_{\parallel}\sim 0.41\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}. We define the B=0B=0 QD pseudo-spin index ς\varsigma from the in-plane symmetry of the wavefunctions. For example, the (H+,H+)(\text{H}{+},\text{H}{+}) sector of the QD Hamiltonian is quadratic in kk and ρ\rho and therefore does not change the parity of the wavefunction in the H+\text{H}{+} sector. On the other hand, the (H+,η+)(\text{H}{+},\upeta{+}) sector is linear in kk and therefore changes the parity of the wavefunction in the sector η+\upeta{+}. The two pseudo-spins are therefore chosen to be (with sector ordering {H+,η+,η−,H−}\{\text{H}{+},\upeta{+},\upeta{-},\text{H}{-}\})

ς=+:|φ⟩\displaystyle\varsigma=+:\ket{\varphi} =[ASAS],\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{A}\\ \mathrm{S}\\ \mathrm{A}\\ \mathrm{S}\end{bmatrix}, ς=−:|φ⟩\displaystyle\varsigma=-:\ket{\varphi} =[SASA],\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{S}\\ \mathrm{A}\\ \mathrm{S}\\ \mathrm{A}\end{bmatrix}, (120)

where the symmetric (S) and antisymmetric (A) parts involve only even jj or odd jj orbital shells, respectively. More explicitly, the ς=+1\varsigma=+1 eigenstates can be expanded in terms of the quantum well subbands |τ​σ;l⟩\ket{\tau\sigma;l} and of the Fock orbitals |j,m⟩\ket{j,m}:

|φi,J,M+⟩=∑l,odd​j,m|H+;l⟩​|j,m⟩​Ai,J,MH;l,j,m+∑l,even​j,m|η+;l⟩​|j,m⟩​Si,J,Mη;l,j,m+∑l,odd​j,m|η−;l⟩|j,m⟩Ai,J,Mη;l,j,m+∑l,even​j,m|H−;l⟩|j,m⟩Si,J,MH;l,j,m,\begin{split}\ket{\varphi_{i,J,M}^{+}}&=\sum_{l,\mathrm{odd}\,j,m}{\ket{\text{H}{+};l}\ket{j,m}A_{i,J,M}^{\text{H}{};l,j,m}}+\sum_{l,\mathrm{even}\,j,m}{\ket{\upeta{+};l}\ket{j,m}S_{i,J,M}^{\upeta{};l,j,m}}\\ &+\sum_{l,\mathrm{odd}\,j,m}{\ket{\upeta{-};l}\ket{j,m}A_{i,J,M}^{\upeta{};l,j,m}}+\sum_{l,\mathrm{even}\,j,m}{\ket{\text{H}{-};l}\ket{j,m}S_{i,J,M}^{\text{H}{};l,j,m}},\end{split} (121)

where ii is a general zz-subband index, and (J,M)(J,M) are general in-plane orbital indices, and where the AA and SS coefficients vanish for even jj or odd jj respectively. The ς=−1\varsigma=-1 pseudo-spin levels are constructed from time reversal rules:

|φi,J,M−⟩=−∑l,odd​j,m|H−;l⟩|j,−m⟩Ai,J,MH;l,j,m+∑l,even​j,m|η−;l⟩|j,−m⟩Si,J,Mη;l,j,m−∑l,odd​j,m|η+;l⟩|j,−m⟩Ai,J,Mη;l,j,m+∑l,even​j,m|H+;l⟩|j,−m⟩Si,J,MH;l,j,m.\begin{split}\ket{\varphi_{i,J,M}^{-}}&=-\sum_{l,\mathrm{odd}\,j,m}{\ket{\text{H}{-};l}\ket{j,-m}A_{i,J,M}^{\text{H}{};l,j,m}}+\sum_{l,\mathrm{even}\,j,m}{\ket{\upeta{-};l}\ket{j,-m}S_{i,J,M}^{\upeta{};l,j,m}}\\ &-\sum_{l,\mathrm{odd}\,j,m}{\ket{\upeta{+};l}\ket{j,-m}A_{i,J,M}^{\upeta{};l,j,m}}+\sum_{l,\mathrm{even}\,j,m}{\ket{\text{H}{+};l}\ket{j,-m}S_{i,J,M}^{\text{H}{};l,j,m}}.\end{split} (122)

We note that the AA and SS coefficients are all real. The quantum dot basis at B=0B=0 is then used to project the full Hamiltonian (29) or (54) onto it. Using the following gauge for the out-of-plane component of the BB-field:

𝐀∥​(𝐫)=B​cos⁡θ2​(−y​𝐞x+x​𝐞y),\mathbf{A}_{\parallel}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{B\cos\theta}{2}\left(-y\mathbf{e}_{x}+x\mathbf{e}_{y}\right), (123)

the full quantum dot Hamiltonian is

𝐇qd(B)=𝐄0qd+α02​lB2[cosθ𝐋2⟂+cos2⁡θ2​lB2𝐋4⟂+sin2⁡θ2​lB2𝐋4∥+sinθ(e−i​ϕ𝐋2∥+sin⁡θ2​lB2e−2​i​ϕ𝐋~4∥+cos⁡θ2​lB2e−i​ϕ𝐋4×+h.c.)],\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{qd}}(B)=\mathbf{E}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}}+\frac{\alpha_{0}}{2l_{B}^{2}}\left[\cos\theta\mathbf{L}_{2\perp}+\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{2l_{B}^{2}}\mathbf{L}_{4\perp}+\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{2l_{B}^{2}}\mathbf{L}_{4\parallel}+\sin\theta\left(e^{-i\phi}\mathbf{L}_{2\parallel}+\frac{\sin\theta}{2l_{B}^{2}}e^{-2i\phi}\tilde{\mathbf{L}}_{4\parallel}+\frac{\cos\theta}{2l_{B}^{2}}e^{-i\phi}\mathbf{L}_{4\times}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\right], (124)

where 𝐄0qd\mathbf{E}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}} are the eigenvalues of ℋ0qd\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}} and the 𝐋\mathbf{L}-matrices are

𝐋2⟂\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{2\perp} =𝐕†[ℳg+2ℳγLz+(2ℳ1ρ−−4iℳ2ρ−k−+h.c.)]𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[\mathcal{M}_{g}+2\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}L_{z}+\left(2\mathcal{M}_{1}\rho_{-}-4i\mathcal{M}_{2}\rho_{-}k_{-}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\right]\mathbf{V}, (125a)
𝐋2∥\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{2\parallel} =𝐕†​[𝒩g−i​𝒩~γ​ρ+−𝒩1+​ρ+​k−−𝒩1−​k−​ρ++(𝒩1++𝒩1−)†​ρ+​k+]​𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[\mathcal{N}_{g}-i\tilde{\mathcal{N}}_{\gamma}\rho_{+}-\mathcal{N}_{1}^{+}\rho_{+}k_{-}-\mathcal{N}_{1}^{-}k_{-}\rho_{+}+\left(\mathcal{N}_{1}^{+}+\mathcal{N}_{1}^{-}\right)^{\dagger}\rho_{+}k_{+}\right]\mathbf{V}, (125b)
𝐋4⟂\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{4\perp} =𝐕†[4ℳγρ−ρ+−4(ℳ2ρ−2+h.c.)]𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[4\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}\rho_{-}\rho_{+}-4\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}\rho_{-}^{2}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\right]\mathbf{V}, (125c)
𝐋4∥\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{4\parallel} =𝐕†​[2​𝒩γ​ρ−​ρ+]​𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[2\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}\rho_{-}\rho_{+}\right]\mathbf{V}, (125d)
𝐋~4∥\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{L}}_{4\parallel} =𝐕†​[−𝒩γ​ρ+2]​𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[-\mathcal{N}_{\gamma}\rho_{+}^{2}\right]\mathbf{V}, (125e)
𝐋4×\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{4\times} =𝐕†​[2​i​(𝒩1++𝒩1−)​ρ−​ρ++2​i​(𝒩1++𝒩1−)†​ρ+2]​𝐕,\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\left[2i\left(\mathcal{N}_{1}^{+}+\mathcal{N}_{1}^{-}\right)\rho_{-}\rho_{+}+2i\left(\mathcal{N}_{1}^{+}+\mathcal{N}_{1}^{-}\right)^{\dagger}\rho_{+}^{2}\right]\mathbf{V}, (125f)

with 𝐕\mathbf{V} the matrix of (column) eigenvectors of ℋ0qd\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\mathrm{qd}}, such that 𝐕†​𝐕=𝟙\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\mathbf{V}=\mathbb{1}.

Figure 7 shows the off-diagonal matrix element xso=|⟨φ1,0,0+|x|φ1,0,0−⟩|x_{\mathrm{so}}=|\braket{\varphi_{1,0,0}^{+}|x|\varphi_{1,0,0}^{-}}| and kso=|⟨φ1,0,0+|kx|φ1,0,0−⟩|k_{\mathrm{so}}=|\braket{\varphi_{1,0,0}^{+}|k_{x}|\varphi_{1,0,0}^{-}}| for the quantum dot ground state orbital with an in-plane magnetic field 𝐁=(0.1​T)​𝐞x\mathbf{B}=(0.1\,\mathrm{T})\mathbf{e}_{x}, and a gate field Fz=1.5​mV/nmF_{z}=1.5\,\mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{nm}.

Similarly, we also plot in Fig. 8, 9 and 10 the longitudinal (σz\sigma_{z}) and the transverse (σx\sigma_{x}) components, in the QD ground state subspace, of the operators that appear in the quadratic expansion of the electrostatic potential underneath the gates (as discussed in the next section) as a function of the magnetic field in-plane angle ϕ\phi.

VII.2 Dephasing time calculations

We consider the dephasing in a quantum dot system where charge traps cause small fluctuations of the gate voltages. The gate layout consists of one square plunger gate of dimension 170​nm×170​nm170\,\mathrm{nm}\times 170\,\mathrm{nm} with a voltage of Vp0=−170​mVV_{p}^{0}=-170\,\mathrm{mV} at the DC operation point. The four identical barrier gates have dimensions 170​nm×50​nm170\,\mathrm{nm}\times 50\,\mathrm{nm}, are separated from the plunger by a 5​nm5\,\mathrm{nm} spacer, and operate at a voltage of Vb0=−70​mVV_{b}^{0}=-70\,\mathrm{mV}. The simulation domain has dimensions 300×300×400​nm300\times 300\times 400\,\mathrm{nm}, with the center of the plunger gate at x,yx,y coordinates (0,0)(0,0) and with the Ge layer starting 20​nm20\,\mathrm{nm} below the surface. The electrostatic potential ϕ\phi is found by solving the Laplace equation

∇⋅[ϵ(𝐫)∇ϕ]\displaystyle\nabla\cdot\left[\epsilon(\mathbf{r})\nabla\phi\right] =0,\displaystyle=0, (126)
⇔[∇2+ϵ′​(z)ϵ⁡(z)​∂∂z]​ϕ\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\left[\nabla^{2}+\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}(z)}{\epsilon(z)}\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\right]\phi =0,\displaystyle=0, (127)

with a mesh size δ​x=δ​y=δ​z=5​nm\delta x=\delta y=\delta z=5\,\mathrm{nm}. We take Dirichlet boundary conditions of 0​mV0\,\mathrm{mV} everywhere except at the surface where the value of ϕ\phi is either 0​mV0\,\mathrm{mV} or set by the corresponding gate voltage. The dielectric constant only depends on zz and is equal to 1616 in Ge and 15.1815.18 in Si0.2Ge0.8 by linear interpolation [2]. The voltages and dimensions mentioned above are such that at (x,y,z)=(0,0,z0)(x,y,z)=(0,0,z_{0}) (where z0≡0​nmz_{0}\equiv 0\,\mathrm{nm} refers to the zz-coordinate in Ge 5​nm5\,\mathrm{nm} below the top Si0.2Ge0.8 barrier), the gate field Fz≈1.487​mV/nmF_{z}\approx 1.487\,\mathrm{mV/\mathrm{nm}}. The corresponding quantum dot effective length is l≈11.2​nml\approx 11.2\,\mathrm{nm}. We write V→=(Vp,V1,V2,V3,V4)\vec{V}=(V_{p},V_{1},V_{2},V_{3},V_{4}) being the voltages of the plunger and of the four barrier gates at +x+x, +y+y, −x-x and −y-y, respectively. In particular, we write for gate ii: Vi=Vi0+δiV_{i}=V_{i}^{0}+\delta_{i}, where Vi0V_{i}^{0} is the DC operation point and δi\delta_{i} is the small fluctuation from noise. We take δi=1​mV\delta_{i}=1\,\mathrm{mV} for each gate, such that T2∗∼1​μ​sT_{2}^{*}\sim 1\,\upmu\mathrm{s} for ε\varepsilon-Ge which is the right order of magnitude for hole spin qubits in Ge [8].

When barrier noise is zero, the general solution of the Poisson equation can be expressed as a linear combination of polynomials that transform according to the trivial irreducible representation of the C4​vC_{4v} point group. Each individual barrier noise further breaks the symmetry of the solution to a linear combination of functions that transform according to the trivial irrep of C1​vC_{1v}. The Poisson equation is linear and therefore the total solution is the sum of the potential generated by each gate:

ϕ⁡(V→,𝐫)=∑i​j[fi​j​(V→0)+hi​j​(δp)]​Ii​(x,y)​zj+∑kzk∑i​jxiyj{[gi​j​k(δ1)+(−1)igi​j​k(δ3)]yj+[gj​i​k(δ2)+(−1)jgj​i​k(δ4)]xi},\begin{split}\phi(\vec{V},\mathbf{r})&=\sum_{ij}{\left[f_{ij}(\vec{V}^{0})+h_{ij}(\delta_{p})\right]I_{i}(x,y)z^{j}}\\ &+\sum_{k}{z^{k}\sum_{ij}{x^{i}y^{j}}\left\{\left[g_{ijk}(\delta_{1})+(-1)^{i}g_{ijk}(\delta_{3})\right]y^{j}+\left[g_{jik}(\delta_{2})+(-1)^{j}g_{jik}(\delta_{4})\right]x^{i}\right\}},\end{split} (128)

where Ii​(x,y)I_{i}(x,y) are invariant functions of the trivial irrep of C4​vC_{4v} (1,x2+y2,(x2−y2)2,x2​y2,…)\left(1,x^{2}+y^{2},(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2},x^{2}y^{2},\dots\right), and fi​jf_{ij}, hi​jh_{ij} and gi​j​kg_{ijk} are expansion coefficients. We Taylor expand the full solution (128) close to the point (0,0,z0)(0,0,z_{0}) to quadratic order (neglecting z2z^{2} terms):

ϕ⁡(V→,𝐫)≈[g100​(δ1)−g100​(δ3)]​x+[g100​(δ2)−g100​(δ4)]​y+[f01​(V→0)+h01​(δp)+g001​(δ1)+g001​(δ2)+g001​(δ3)+g001​(δ4)]​z+[f10​(V→0)+h10​(δp)+g200​(δ1)+g010​(δ2)+g200​(δ3)+g010​(δ4)]​x2+[f10​(V→0)+h10​(δp)+g010​(δ1)+g200​(δ2)+g010​(δ3)+g200​(δ4)]​y2+[g101​(δ1)−g101​(δ3)]​z​x+[g101​(δ2)−g101​(δ4)]​y​z.\begin{split}\phi(\vec{V},\mathbf{r})&\approx\left[g_{100}(\delta_{1})-g_{100}(\delta_{3})\right]x+\left[g_{100}(\delta_{2})-g_{100}(\delta_{4})\right]y\\ &+\left[f_{01}(\vec{V}^{0})+h_{01}(\delta_{p})+g_{001}(\delta_{1})+g_{001}(\delta_{2})+g_{001}(\delta_{3})+g_{001}(\delta_{4})\right]z\\ &+\left[f_{10}(\vec{V}^{0})+h_{10}(\delta_{p})+g_{200}(\delta_{1})+g_{010}(\delta_{2})+g_{200}(\delta_{3})+g_{010}(\delta_{4})\right]x^{2}\\ &+\left[f_{10}(\vec{V}^{0})+h_{10}(\delta_{p})+g_{010}(\delta_{1})+g_{200}(\delta_{2})+g_{010}(\delta_{3})+g_{200}(\delta_{4})\right]y^{2}\\ &+\left[g_{101}(\delta_{1})-g_{101}(\delta_{3})\right]zx+\left[g_{101}(\delta_{2})-g_{101}(\delta_{4})\right]yz.\end{split} (129)

Note that x​yxy-terms are forbidden by symmetry. When the fluctuations δ→\vec{\delta} are small, the full solution can be expressed in terms of the fluctuations δi\delta_{i} multiplied by the derivative of the expansion coefficients close to the DC operation point, i.e. gi​j​k​(δ)≈gi​j​k′​(0)​δg_{ijk}(\delta)\approx g_{ijk}^{\prime}(0)\delta. Applying this and casting the full solution close to the point (0,0,z0)(0,0,z_{0}) in terms of harmonic oscillator parameters we obtain

ϕ⁡(𝐫)≈Fz​z+1e​α0l4​(x2+y2)+g100′​(0)​(δ1−δ3)​x+g100′​(0)​(δ2−δ4)​y+[h01′​(0)​δp+g001′​(0)​(δ1+δ2+δ3+δ4)]​z+[h10′​(0)​δp+12​(g200′​(0)+g010′​(0))​(δ1+δ2+δ3+δ4)]​(x2+y2)+12​(g200′​(0)−g010′​(0))​(δ1−δ2+δ3−δ4)​(x2−y2)+g101′​(0)​(δ1−δ3)​z​x+g101′​(0)​(δ2−δ4)​y​z,\begin{split}\phi(\mathbf{r})&\approx F_{z}z+\frac{1}{e}\frac{\alpha_{0}}{l^{4}}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)\\ &+g_{100}^{\prime}(0)(\delta_{1}-\delta_{3})x+g_{100}^{\prime}(0)(\delta_{2}-\delta_{4})y+\left[h_{01}^{\prime}(0)\delta_{p}+g_{001}^{\prime}(0)\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}+\delta_{3}+\delta_{4}\right)\right]z\\ &+\left[h_{10}^{\prime}(0)\delta_{p}+\frac{1}{2}\left(g_{200}^{\prime}(0)+g_{010}^{\prime}(0)\right)\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}+\delta_{3}+\delta_{4}\right)\right]\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)\\ &+\frac{1}{2}\left(g_{200}^{\prime}(0)-g_{010}^{\prime}(0)\right)\left(\delta_{1}-\delta_{2}+\delta_{3}-\delta_{4}\right)\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right)\\ &+g_{101}^{\prime}(0)(\delta_{1}-\delta_{3})zx+g_{101}^{\prime}(0)(\delta_{2}-\delta_{4})yz,\end{split} (130)

where Fz=f01​(V→0)F_{z}=f_{01}(\vec{V}^{0}) and α0/l4=e​f10​(V→0)\alpha_{0}/l^{4}=ef_{10}(\vec{V}^{0}). The Larmor frequency shifts εi\varepsilon_{i} of the qubit for gate ii can then be computed directly from the seven constants h01′​(0)h_{01}^{\prime}(0), h10′​(0)h_{10}^{\prime}(0), g100′​(0)g_{100}^{\prime}(0), g001′​(0)g_{001}^{\prime}(0), g200′​(0)g_{200}^{\prime}(0), g010′​(0)g_{010}^{\prime}(0) and g101′​(0)g_{101}^{\prime}(0), and the σz\sigma_{z}-component in the qubit subspace of the position operators x2+y2x^{2}+y^{2}, x2−y2x^{2}-y^{2}, xx, yy, zz, z​xzx and y​zyz (see Fig. 8, 9 and 10). At the DC operation point, we find the following constants:

h01′​(0)\displaystyle h_{01}^{\prime}(0) =−9.4340⋅10−3nm−1,\displaystyle=-9.4340\cdot 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}, (131a)
h10′​(0)\displaystyle h_{10}^{\prime}(0) =−1.8569⋅10−5nm−2,\displaystyle=-1.8569\cdot 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}, (131b)
g100′​(0)\displaystyle g_{100}^{\prime}(0) =3.9668⋅10−4​nm−1,\displaystyle=3.9668\cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}, (131c)
g001′​(0)\displaystyle g_{001}^{\prime}(0) =4.1757⋅10−4​nm−1,\displaystyle=4.1757\cdot 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}, (131d)
g200′​(0)\displaystyle g_{200}^{\prime}(0) =6.1099⋅10−6​nm−2,\displaystyle=6.1099\cdot 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}, (131e)
g010′​(0)\displaystyle g_{010}^{\prime}(0) =−8.9887⋅10−7nm−2,\displaystyle=-8.9887\cdot 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}, (131f)

Fig. 11 shows the solution of the Poisson equation on the simulation domain described at the beginning of this section.

Assuming the plunger gate and the four barriers act as uncorrelated sources of 1/f1/f charge noise, the dephasing time T2∗T_{2}^{*} is equal to

T2∗=ℏ∑iεi2​π∫ωc​t/2∞d​x​sin2⁡(x)x3,T_{2}^{*}=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\int_{\omega_{c}t/2}^{\infty}{dx\,\frac{\sin^{2}(x)}{x^{3}}}}}, (132)

where the sum is made on all 55 sources of noise, tt is the measurement time and ωc\omega_{c} is a cut-off frequency. If ωc​t≈0.10879\omega_{c}t\approx 0.10879 the integral is close to π\pi and the square-root term ≈1\approx 1.

Plots of the T2∗T_{2}^{*} for the three systems as a function of the BB-field in-plane angle ϕ\phi are shown in Fig. 12. The two sharp peaks in the spiked Ge appear due to the vanishing of the longitudinal component of zz and x2+y2x^{2}+y^{2}, see Fig. 10.

VIII Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimisation Methodology

The optimisation problem considered here involves simultaneously maximising two competing objectives over a multi-dimensional continuous input space. A Bayesian optimisation (BO) framework is employed. BO maintains a cheap-to-evaluate probabilistic surrogate model that is updated after every batch of simulation calls, and uses an acquisition function to decide which candidate points to evaluate next. The specific variant used here is a multi-objective Bayesian optimisation loop based on a Multitask Gaussian Process (MTGP) surrogate and a Pareto Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) acquisition strategy.

VIII.1 Optimisation Objectives

Let 𝐱∈𝒳⊂ℝN\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} be the input vector. The two scalar objectives evaluated by the MATLAB oracle fsbf_{\mathrm{sb}} are

f1​(𝐱)=|b2​(𝐱)|,f2​(𝐱)=log⁡(1.|∂b2(2)​(𝐱)|),f_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\bigl|b_{2}(\mathbf{x})\bigr|,\qquad f_{2}(\mathbf{x})=\log\left(\frac{1.}{\bigl|\partial b_{2}^{(2)}(\mathbf{x})\bigr|}\right), (133)

where b2b_{2} and ∂b2(2)\partial b_{2}^{(2)} are two output quantities returned by the simulation. For the bump system we consider ∂b2(2)\partial b_{2}^{(2)}, for the spike system we consider ∂b2\partial b_{2} Both objectives are to be maximised simultaneously, forming a Pareto front in the objective space ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}.

VIII.2 Input Space and Candidate Pool

The NN input variables together with their admissible ranges are listed in Table 3 and  4 for the two systems under scrutiny (Si bump and Si spike). All variables are treated as continuous. At the start of each optimisation run a candidate pool of Ncand=50,000N_{\mathrm{cand}}=50{,}000 points is sampled independently and uniformly at random from the Cartesian product of the intervals in Table 3. Evaluated points are removed from the pool after each BO iteration so that no point is selected and evaluated twice.

The range for the gate electric field FzF_{z} is chosen such that the ground state is located in Ge, not in the triangular potential formed at the surface in the Si1-xGex barrier. We first define the mapping r∈[0,1]↦Fz​(r)∈[Fz−,Fz+]r\in[0,1]\mapsto F_{z}(r)\in[F_{z}^{-},F_{z}^{+}], where

Fz​(r)=10(1−r)​fmin+r​fmax​mV/nm.F_{z}(r)=10^{(1-r)f_{\mathrm{min}}+rf_{\mathrm{max}}}\,\mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{nm}. (134)

For the lower bound we take fmin=−1f_{\mathrm{min}}=-1 such that Fz−=Fz​(r=0)≡0.1​mV/nmF_{z}^{-}=F_{z}(r=0)\equiv 0.1\,\mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{nm}, which always returns a ground state in Ge for our parameter space. The upper bound Fz+​(di,ε∥,A,…)F_{z}^{+}(d_{i},\varepsilon_{\parallel},A,\dots) generally depends on the heterostructure parameters. A sufficient condition for a ground state in Ge is to ensure that the energy of the LH band at the surface remains higher than that of the HH band just underneath the bump or below the second spike (assuming the Si1-xGex barrier is tensile strained and Ge is compressive strained). If LL is the thickness of the Si1-xGex barrier, then FzF_{z} must be smaller than

Fz<Fz+=1e​ESiGe−EGeL+ℓ,F_{z}<F_{z}^{+}=\frac{1}{e}\frac{E_{\mathrm{SiGe}}-E_{\mathrm{Ge}}}{L+\ell}, (135)

where ℓ=d+w+4​τ−\ell=d+w+4\tau_{-} for bumped Ge++ and ℓ=d2+0.5​nm\ell=d_{2}+0.5\,\mathrm{nm} for spiked Ge++. The band edge energies are

EGe\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{Ge}} =ℰΓ5+Ge+Δ0Ge3+avGe​Tr​εGe+bGe​δ​εGe,\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma_{5}^{+}}^{\mathrm{Ge}}+\frac{\Delta_{0}^{\mathrm{Ge}}}{3}+a_{v}^{\mathrm{Ge}}\text{Tr}\,\varepsilon^{\mathrm{Ge}}+b^{\mathrm{Ge}}\delta\varepsilon^{\mathrm{Ge}}, (136)
ESiGe\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{SiGe}} =ℰΓ5+SiGe+Δ0SiGe3+avSiGe​Tr​εSiGe+Δ0SiGe2​(1−2​ρ+9​ρ2−ρ−1),\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma_{5}^{+}}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}+\frac{\Delta_{0}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}}{3}+a_{v}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}\text{Tr}\,\varepsilon^{\mathrm{SiGe}}+\frac{\Delta_{0}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}}{2}\left(\sqrt{1-2\rho+9\rho^{2}}-\rho-1\right), (137)

where ρ=bSiGe​δ​εSiGe/Δ0SiGe\rho=b^{\mathrm{SiGe}}\delta\varepsilon^{\mathrm{SiGe}}/\Delta_{0}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}. It is straightforward to verify that the last term in ESiGeE_{\mathrm{SiGe}} tends to −bSiGe​δ​εSiGe-b^{\mathrm{SiGe}}\delta\varepsilon^{\mathrm{SiGe}} in the limit Δ0SiGe→∞\Delta_{0}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}\to\infty, as expected for a LH band in the limit of infinite bulk SOI. The strain components in the SiGe layer are determined from the in-plane lattice constant of the strained Ge layer, assuming a coherent growth:

ε∥SiGe=(1+ε∥Ge)​a0Gea0SiGe−1,\varepsilon_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}=\frac{(1+\varepsilon_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{Ge}})a_{0}^{\mathrm{Ge}}}{a_{0}^{\mathrm{SiGe}}}-1, (138)

with a0a_{0} being the lattice constant of the respective material without strain. Then we take the logarithm of Fz+F_{z}^{+} to obtain fmax=log10⁡[Fz+/(mV/nm)]f_{\mathrm{max}}=\log_{10}[F_{z}^{+}/(\mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{nm})].

VIII.3 Model specification

The surrogate is an Exact Multitask Gaussian Process (MTGP) implemented in GPyTorch [9]. An MTGP models the two objectives jointly, allowing the model to exploit inter-task correlations. Formally, the joint prior over outputs 𝐟⁡(𝐱)=[f1​(𝐱),f2​(𝐱)]⊤\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=[f_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\,f_{2}(\mathbf{x})]^{\top} is a Multitask Multivariate Normal distribution:

p⁡(𝐟⁡(𝐱))=𝒩⁡(𝝁⁡(𝐱),𝐊⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)),p\!\left(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bm{\mu}(\mathbf{x}),\;\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\right), (139)

where the mean and covariance are structured as described below.

Mean function.

A MultitaskMean composed of independent ConstantMean functions is used per task:

μt​(𝐱)=ct,t∈{1,2},\mu_{t}(\mathbf{x})=c_{t},\qquad t\in\{1,2\}, (140)

with learned constants c1,c2∈ℝc_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}.

Covariance (kernel) function.

The joint covariance is constructed via the MultitaskKernel of rank R=2R=2:

k⁡((𝐱,t),(𝐱′,t′))=kRBF​(𝐱,𝐱′)⋅Bt​t′,k\bigl((\mathbf{x},t),\,(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\bigr)=k_{\mathrm{RBF}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\cdot B_{tt^{\prime}}, (141)

where kRBFk_{\mathrm{RBF}} is the Radial Basis Function (squared-exponential) kernel

kRBF(𝐱,𝐱′)=σf2exp(−12∑j=19(xj−xj′)2ℓj2),k_{\mathrm{RBF}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\sigma_{f}^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{9}\frac{(x_{j}-x^{\prime}_{j})^{2}}{\ell_{j}^{2}}\right), (142)

and 𝐁∈ℝ2×2\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} is a positive semi-definite task covariance matrix parameterised as 𝐁=𝐯𝐯⊤+diag⁡(𝜿)\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^{\top}+\mathrm{diag}(\bm{\kappa}) for a rank-2 vector 𝐯∈ℝ2\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and noise variances 𝜿\bm{\kappa}. The learnable parameters of the kernel are the output scale σf2\sigma_{f}^{2}, the nine length-scales ℓ1,…,ℓ9\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{9}, and the task covariance parameters 𝐯\mathbf{v} and 𝜿\bm{\kappa}.

Likelihood.

A MultitaskGaussianLikelihood with per-task homoscedastic noise σnoise,t2\sigma_{\mathrm{noise},t}^{2} is assumed:

yt​(𝐱)=ft​(𝐱)+εt,εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σnoise,t2).y_{t}(\mathbf{x})=f_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{noise},t}^{2}). (143)

A Cholesky jitter of 10−310^{-3} is added to the diagonal of the kernel matrix to ensure numerical stability during factorisation.

VIII.4 Training

At every BO iteration the hyperparameters are re-estimated by maximising the Exact Marginal Log-Likelihood (MLL):

log⁡p⁡(𝐘∣𝐗,𝜽)=−12​𝐲⊤​𝐊𝜽−1​𝐲−12​log​det𝐊𝜽−n2​log​2​π,\log p(\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{X},\bm{\theta})=-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}_{\bm{\theta}}^{-1}\mathbf{y}-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\mathbf{K}_{\bm{\theta}}-\tfrac{n}{2}\log 2\pi, (144)

where 𝐲\mathbf{y} is the stacked vector of all observed outputs, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is the matrix of training inputs, and 𝜽\bm{\theta} collects all kernel and noise hyperparameters. Optimisation is performed with the Adam optimiser [10] using

  • •

    learning rate α=0.05\alpha=0.05,

  • •

    NGP=200N_{\mathrm{GP}}=200 gradient steps per BO iteration,

VIII.5 Data Normalisation

Input normalisation.

All nine input features are normalised using StandardScaler (zero mean, unit variance), fitted on the full training set available at each iteration and re-fitted each time the training data is extended:

x~j=xj−μ^xjσ^xj.\tilde{x}_{j}=\frac{x_{j}-\hat{\mu}_{x_{j}}}{\hat{\sigma}_{x_{j}}}. (145)

Output normalisation.

Each of the two output columns is standardised independently using its own StandardScaler, again re-fitted at every iteration:

y~t=yt−μ^ytσ^yt,t∈{1,2}.\tilde{y}_{t}=\frac{y_{t}-\hat{\mu}_{y_{t}}}{\hat{\sigma}_{y_{t}}},\qquad t\in\{1,2\}. (146)

The GP is trained entirely in the normalised space. Predictions are mapped back to the original scale before computing acquisition values and before recording results.

VIII.6 Acquisition Function: Pareto UCB

For each candidate point 𝐱\mathbf{x} and each task tt, the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) is computed from the GP posterior as

UCBt​(𝐱)=μt​(𝐱)+β​σt​(𝐱),\mathrm{UCB}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\beta\,\sigma_{t}(\mathbf{x}), (147)

where μt​(𝐱)\mu_{t}(\mathbf{x}) and σt​(𝐱)\sigma_{t}(\mathbf{x}) are the posterior mean and standard deviation (in the original output scale, after inverse transform), and β≥0\beta\geq 0 is an exploration–exploitation trade-off parameter, here set =1.0=1.0.

The UCB values are then assembled into a two-dimensional acquisition vector:

𝐮⁡(𝐱)=[UCB1​(𝐱),UCB2​(𝐱)]⊤.\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})=\bigl[\mathrm{UCB}_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\;\mathrm{UCB}_{2}(\mathbf{x})\bigr]^{\top}. (148)

A point 𝐱\mathbf{x} is said to Pareto-dominate 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} with respect to 𝐮\mathbf{u} if ut​(𝐱)≥ut​(𝐱′)u_{t}(\mathbf{x})\geq u_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) for all tt and ut​(𝐱)>ut​(𝐱′)u_{t}(\mathbf{x})>u_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) for at least one tt. The Pareto front of the candidate pool is the set of non-dominated points:

𝒫={𝐱∈𝒳cand:∄𝐱′∈𝒳cand s.t. 𝐮(𝐱′) dominates 𝐮(𝐱)}.\mathcal{P}=\bigl\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{cand}}:\nexists\,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{cand}}\text{ s.t.\ }\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\text{ dominates }\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})\bigr\}. (149)

All points on the UCB Pareto front 𝒫\mathcal{P} are selected as the next batch to evaluate. The selected points are removed from the candidate pool before the next iteration begins.

VIII.7 Computational performance

Model training and inference is performed on a MacBook Pro, M3 Chip, 18GB Memory. In light of the feasibility of the study with this computational equipment, detailed performance analysis and optimization were deemed beyond the scope of the work. In its current implementation, training time at each Bayesian Optimization iteration is in the 10110^{1} seconds order of magnitude, inference is 10210^{2} faster w.r.t. the physics based ground-truth approach.
